name: KubeVista
alt: KubeVista operations console showing its validated deployment snapshot
summary: A Kubernetes operations console backed by an EKS platform I built and tested on AWS.
detail: I built the Go API and React dashboard, then the platform around them: networking, identity, GitOps, telemetry, and failure tests. Inventory stays read-only by default. A separate operator path can restart or scale an approved Deployment without opening the door to arbitrary Kubernetes writes.
bullets: Restart and scale are the only write actions, limited by namespace and replica guardrails.
Every change requires a reason, Kubernetes dry run, current resource version, and single-use review plan.
Production execution verifies the load balancer's signed identity claims and records an audit receipt.
All 896 requests returned HTTP 200 during a two-second API pod replacement.
note: The August AWS run used the read-only version. Guarded operations were added afterward and are available in the local simulation; the paid cluster remains intentionally offline.

ownership.scope: Product, Go API, React interface, AWS platform, delivery, security boundaries, and operations
ownership.status: Guarded operations tested locally; paid AWS environment retired

architecture.alt: KubeVista architecture from GitHub Actions through Argo CD into a private EKS node group, with AWS ingress, pod identity, secrets, and an observability stack
architecture.caption: Read-only inventory is the baseline. Restart and scale use a smaller, explicitly enabled operator role with a review gate in front of it.
architecture.how: Terraform builds the VPC, EKS control plane, managed node group, KMS keys, and AWS integrations. GitHub Actions publishes a scanned and signed image; Argo CD reconciles the manifests. Traffic enters through an AWS load balancer. The Go API reads inventory with its baseline permissions, while an optional namespaced role permits only Deployment restart and scale after a server-side dry run.
decisions: The browser never submits YAML. It chooses between two typed operations, supplies a reason, and reviews the exact effect before execution.
Review plans expire after five minutes, work once, and are bound to the request and Kubernetes resource version to prevent edits or replay.
The operator role remains namespaced and cannot read Secrets, exec into pods, change RBAC, delete resources, or write arbitrary objects.

caseStudy.title: How a change gets through
caseStudy.intro: The write path is deliberately narrower than the inventory API. Each stage removes a class of accidental or unauthorized change before Kubernetes accepts it.

steps.title: Choose
steps.text: Select restart or scale for a Deployment in an allowed namespace and explain why the change is needed.

steps.title: Constrain
steps.text: The API rejects unsupported kinds, namespaces, actions, and replica counts before touching the cluster.

steps.title: Dry run
steps.text: Kubernetes authorization and admission evaluate the same request without persisting it.

steps.title: Bind
steps.text: A five-minute, single-use plan locks the reviewed request to the current resource version.

steps.title: Execute
steps.text: The API rechecks identity and dry run, applies the change through scoped RBAC, and records a receipt.

architecture.outcome: Twelve Argo CD applications were Synced and Healthy, and all 896 requests returned HTTP 200 while an API pod was replaced. The paid AWS environment was then torn down and checked for leftovers.

name: Illuma
summary: A college admissions platform for researching schools, reviewing essays, and building a college list.
detail: I founded Illuma and built its AI tools and admissions probability model. The tools share state and validate their outputs before passing results to the next step.
bullets: 39 typed tools with shared state and deterministic validation.
Admissions modeling across 130 universities.
79,000 applicant outcomes underpin the platform.
Grew to more than 5,000 users.
note: Product figures are from my September 2026 résumé.

ownership.scope: Product direction, agent system, admissions model, and platform implementation

architecture.alt: Illuma architecture showing a student workspace, an agent coordinator, research and writing tools, shared state and validation, and admissions data and prediction services
architecture.caption: A coordinated tool system: each specialist works against the same student context instead of producing isolated chat responses.
architecture.how: A student request enters a coordinator that selects typed tools for school research, college-list planning, or essay review. Every tool reads and updates shared application state, and deterministic checks gate what can move to the next step. The prediction path combines a student profile with historical applicant outcomes and university data.
decisions: Typed tool inputs and outputs make handoffs inspectable and reject malformed results early.
Shared state keeps recommendations consistent across research, essays, and the evolving college list.
Admissions prediction is kept as a separate data pipeline rather than hidden inside an unconstrained language-model answer.
architecture.outcome: The product grew to more than 5,000 users, with 39 typed tools and admissions modeling across 130 universities using 79,000 applicant outcomes.

name: Ledgly
alt: Ledgly financial dashboard with charges, payments, and membership balances
summary: A shared ledger that helps club treasurers match payment emails to dues. Fewer spreadsheet detective stories.
detail: I built the member ledger, payment reconciliation, and review workflow. Charges, payments, expenses, and allocations are separate records, so partial payments and split allocations have somewhere sensible to go.
bullets: Gmail ingestion matches payment notices to members and records confidence for review.
Organization-scoped roles are enforced by the API.
The assistant proposes financial changes for confirmation before executing them.
Before-and-after audit records support batch undo and redo.
note: Dashboard image from the project repository.

ownership.scope: Architecture, ledger model, reconciliation, permissions, and audit workflow

architecture.alt: Ledgly architecture showing the Next.js interface, NestJS API, PostgreSQL ledger, Gmail ingestion, and a review gate before financial records are changed
architecture.caption: Incoming payment email becomes a proposed ledger match, not an automatic financial fact.
architecture.how: The Next.js client calls an organization-scoped NestJS API backed by Prisma and PostgreSQL. A Gmail worker reads payment notices, extracts candidate transactions, and proposes member matches with confidence. Treasurers review ambiguous matches before payments are allocated to charges; the API records the before-and-after state in the audit log.
decisions: Charges, payments, expenses, and allocations are separate records so partial and split payments remain representable.
Gmail is read-only, and low-confidence matches stop at a human review queue.
AI write tools require confirmation and use the same role checks and audit path as ordinary API actions.
architecture.outcome: The extra review step gives up fully automatic reconciliation in exchange for traceable financial changes, reversible batches, and fewer silent misallocations.

name: Sizzle
summary: Recipes with an interactive kitchen counter. The ingredients have actual physics.
detail: A dish name or a few ingredients become a saved recipe and a step-by-step cooking view. I built structured recipe generation, background illustration jobs, and the Matter.js counter.
bullets: Structured ingredients, equipment, and steps drive the interface.
Matter.js handles gravity, collisions, and ingredient placement.
Supabase stores recipes; OCI Object Storage holds the generated step illustrations.

ownership.scope: Recipe pipeline, FastAPI service, interactive cooking view, and OCI deployment

architecture.alt: Sizzle pipeline from a dish or ingredient prompt through recipe lookup and structured generation to Supabase, image jobs, OCI Object Storage, and a Matter.js cooking view
architecture.caption: The recipe is usable before the slower illustration jobs finish.
architecture.how: A natural-language request first searches saved recipes. If nothing fits, FastAPI creates structured ingredients, equipment, and steps, persists them in Supabase, and starts illustration work in the background. The Next.js cooking view renders each step and uses Matter.js to place the relevant objects on a virtual counter.
decisions: Recipe generation produces a fixed structure so the interface does not have to parse prose.
Image work runs after the recipe is saved, keeping the main request independent of slower media generation.
Matter.js owns placement and collision behavior while React owns the recipe and step state.
architecture.outcome: A recipe can still load when image generation or object storage fails; the cost is accepting partially illustrated recipes and reporting those jobs separately.

name: Academis
videoAlt: Academis demo moving from the AP Economics study desk into the Biology course workspace
summary: An AP study app that answers questions from the selected course material.
detail: I built subject-scoped retrieval and a study interface for textbooks, questions, quizzes, and graphs. Microeconomics and Macroeconomics are the most complete courses; science content is partial.
bullets: PDF extraction, chunking, and embeddings feed MongoDB Atlas Vector Search.
FastAPI separates tutoring, retrieval, quiz generation, and graph generation.
Firebase Authentication protects student routes.

ownership.scope: Document ingestion, retrieval, tutoring API, and study interface

architecture.alt: Academis retrieval architecture showing PDF ingestion into subject-tagged chunks and MongoDB Atlas Vector Search, then a student question retrieving context for answer generation
architecture.caption: Ingestion and question answering meet at the subject-scoped vector index.
architecture.how: An upload script extracts textbook PDFs, splits them into chunks, creates embeddings, and stores subject metadata with each record in MongoDB Atlas. At question time, FastAPI searches only the selected course, assembles the closest passages, and sends that context into the tutoring answer path used by the React interface.
decisions: Subject metadata constrains retrieval so a macroeconomics answer cannot silently borrow biology context.
Ingestion is a separate command-line pipeline, keeping expensive document processing out of student requests.
Tutoring, quizzes, graphs, and textbook routes remain separate FastAPI modules even though they share course data.
architecture.outcome: Microeconomics and Macroeconomics have the most complete material. Science course shells remain visible but are described as partial rather than overstated as finished.

name: FilmVault
videoAlt: FilmVault demo showing live movie data, people browsing, member picks, ratings, and saved collections
summary: Films, television, ratings, and saved collections—with live catalog data from TMDB.
detail: I built the original FilmVault before using generative-AI coding tools, and have since revisited the interface and local setup. TMDB supplies catalog data; the app owns accounts, ratings, and collections.
bullets: Express combines TMDB search and recommendations with member-owned data.
Registration, email verification, password recovery, and JWT authorization.
MySQL in the original design, plus SQLite for repeatable local demos.
Terraform defines the original OCI infrastructure, including networking, secrets, and access controls.

ownership.scope: React client, Express API, member data, TMDB integration, and original OCI design
ownership.status: Recorded local demo; historical cloud design

architecture.alt: FilmVault architecture showing a React client calling an Express API that combines TMDB catalog data with member accounts, ratings, collections, email, and OCI storage
architecture.caption: Catalog metadata stays external; FilmVault owns the social layer around it.
architecture.how: The React client uses one Express API for searches, people, authentication, profiles, ratings, and collections. The API enriches member-owned records with TMDB movie and television metadata, sends account email, and can process profile images before writing them to OCI Object Storage.
decisions: TMDB remains the catalog source while the application database owns users, ratings, and saved collections.
Authentication and admin checks live in API middleware rather than being inferred from client state.
The current SQLite demo path improves repeatability; the original OCI design retains MySQL and broader infrastructure.
architecture.outcome: The local demo is cheap and reproducible, while the checked-in OCI design shows the original production boundary. That history also leaves dependency upgrades and fresh deployment validation as explicit maintenance work.

name: Summit Tutoring Center
summary: A working website for a tutoring center, with schedules the staff can update themselves.
detail: I built this for a tutoring business owned by family friends. It covers classes, staff, counseling, and inquiries, and fits the hosting setup they already had.
bullets: Staff maintain schedules, seminars, and posts through published Google Sheets.
CSV parsing handles quoted and multiline fields, with caching and stale-data fallback.
The inquiry flow uses Web3Forms when configured and falls back to an email draft.
Deployed to the business’s existing DreamHost account.

ownership.scope: Information architecture, frontend, staff-managed content flow, and deployment

architecture.alt: Summit Tutoring Center publishing flow from staff-managed Google Sheets through CSV parsing and browser caching to the React website on DreamHost
architecture.caption: A deliberately small publishing system that the business can operate without a CMS.
architecture.how: Staff edit schedules, seminars, and posts in familiar Google Sheets. The React site fetches the published CSV, parses quoted and multiline fields, and keeps the latest good response in browser storage. The production build stays on the business's existing DreamHost account.
decisions: Google Sheets serves as the editing interface, avoiding a custom CMS and new staff accounts.
A five-minute cache limits repeat fetches while stale-data fallback keeps the last valid schedule visible.
The inquiry form uses Web3Forms when configured and can fall back to an email draft.
architecture.outcome: The site is live for a real tutoring business, and nontechnical staff can update frequently changing information without asking for a code deployment.
